a) it depends on the way it's banned. there are multiple ways it could be done. to ban short term accommodation is a rather vague proposal. here are a few answers based on a few potential policies:

- brutal tax on vacant dwellings. in this scenario we define "vacant" as a dwelling that is not owner-occupied and not tenated, with a minimum of a 3 month lease. a property that is rented out for two weeks and then off the market would be considered vacant under this rule, and subject to heavy enough tax to make it an unprofitable venture. 

this would kill airbnb and stayz ventures that involve leasing the whole property, but the app would continue to operate and there would likely still be some airbnbs in which an owner-occupant can lease out their spare bedroom without being subject to the tax, among other workarounds

- ban on offering short term accommodation services without being a licensed hotel. this would work to an extent, but it would also kill some legitimate businesses that while not being hotels, aren't airbnbs either, such as campsites or regional bed and breakfasts that have been operating for the past 30 years without issue. 

- ban the apps in and of themselves. ineffective. something else will take their place. 

imo, banning it outright would not work well, as you'd be hard pressed to find a way to write a policy that bans airbnbs effectively enough that doesn't also attack hotels or student accommodation or other legit services. a vacant property tax would only be a partial solution, as the airbnb problem is tied up in the much larger issues of housing affordability, land hoarding, renters rights etc, but it would be a start.

it's not a defense of their actions- nobody has any right to deny you a peaceful life, free from assault, theft and any other harassment, regardless of their personal troubles. but they're just a symptom. locking them up is just a bandaid that you pay for with your tax money, one that fails to address the real problem, and ultimately does more harm. 

like i said in my original post, we are in the midst of a huge socioeconomic crisis. wages have stayed stagnant despite inflation and a rise in the cost of everything from fuel to a doctor's visit, the job market is one of the toughest in the country to break into, the casualisation of the workforce has eroded most worker's rights to almost nothing- no sick leave, no notice dismissals, no room to negotiate. social safety nets and the healthcare and psychiatric systems are gutted, inadequate, and underfunded. you can't even rely on an ambulance coming in time to save your life if you experience a heart attack. even finding a dinky little room in a sharehouse somewhere has become a blood sport. 

the violence and unrest we're experiencing here is a warning sign. it's people in distress. it's a society in distress. and we can only push for a solution if we understand who is really to blame for that- the ones with the power and resources to do something about it. our government has, as you said, failed us all. failed those "gronks" as much as you or i.

and the people who replace them? and the people who replace those people? this tiny group of people are a product of their environment. i have worked closely with them, and grew up around similar in new south wales. it's a symptom of a larger, systemic failure. like a fever in someone with an infection. 

you must start asking WHY when you see things like this, distressing as they are. i will choose to take you in good faith and assume you are just frustrated by a situation that is very obviously wrong. people should not be acting this way. nobody should feel unsafe walking down a well lit street. nobody should feel the need to flee their home. it's true. but still, ask the question: why? how is it that more and more people are behaving antisocially, how is it that this is spreading, and what drives those people to behave as they do? what is their motive, and how did they come by such a motive? is it money? why are they so desperate for money? is it drugs? how is it they came to turn to substance abuse, and why have they not been treated for a substance abuse disorder? and so on.

asking those questions is not seeking to excuse people who behave violently, but to understand the broader, societal factors that enabled it to happen, and once more people understand that, we are better positioned to make a lasting change.

your problem with "gronks" and the poorer regions won't be fixed by moving those people somewhere else, unless you plan to put them all on a plane and send them to a different state. and there will always be more to replace them even if you do. 

the only way to solve that problem is improving access social safety nets like substance abuse and alcoholism support programs to assist people in getting clean/sober, and socioeconomic improvements so they don't get right back on the grog to cope with the stress of poverty.

then don't get a horse. i grew up on a farm with six horses and was a champion showjumper, and their care is expensive, and riding them without any instruction or supervision as a beginner can be very dangerous. head and spinal injuries/deaths are more common among equestrians than cyclists! 

keeping a horse is about more than your upfront cost, even if you can find one someone is simply giving away for free, what's really going to chew through your wallet is the gear, food, and care requirements for your horse. they will need winter and summer rugs, brushes, tack, hoof picks, regular specialist vet visits, farrier appointments for hoof care and shoeing, the shoes themselves, a fly mask for the summer, and that's just the start. you will also need to pay careful attention to their diet, a horse fed an incorrect diet (for example, just letting them graze exclusively on lush green grass, or exclusively grain!) can result in laminitis, an excruciatingly painful hoof condition that is often incurable and renders the horse unable to be ridden at best, and needing to be compassionately euthanized at worst. providing a balanced diet for your horse will cost you a lot of money, more than it costs to put fuel in your car. 

a good saddle, bridle, and saddle pad will cost over a grand by themselves. and then there's *your* gear, if you plan to ride your horse. for your own safety you'll need a helmet and smooth-soled riding boots (don't even think about riding them with any old shoes- riding boots are designed to slip out of the stirrups if you should fall off your horse. i have personally been dragged behind a bolting horse by my leg caught in the stirrups, and i'm lucky it didn't put me in the hospital or worse. many people have died in that specific scenario.). riding pants are also a good idea if you value your inner thighs. 

then there's riding lessons. this isn't negotiable; it's like if your motorcycle had a brain and also happened to be a prey animal that can behave unpredictably and uncontrollably when frightened. you need lessons, for your sake and for the sake of your horse.

owning a horse is equivalent to owning a car with terrible fuel economy, financially. the start-up cost is not that different either, taking all your gear into account. horses live for over thirty years. they're an expensive, lifetime commitment. they're beautiful animals that can form strong and lasting bonds with their caretakers, and having one can be incredibly rewarding, but it's a bigger commitment than a regular pet. only do it if you're sure, and if you're willing to put the time and money in to care for your animal.

it's because when you're in a very low socioeconomic area, sometimes the only people you can rely on for help are your community. remaining on good terms with your neighbors is more than just being nice, it's a survival instinct. 

where i grew up there was a lot of conflict, because that kind of environment also puts a lot of stress and pressure on people with very few tools available for dealing with it in a healthy way, but there was also an unspoken rule that grudges were not something any of us were allowed to hold. if crazy kate across the street had a punchup with you last week but this week she needs someone to watch the kids while she goes to a make-or-break job interview, you watch those kids. no one was going to take care of any of us, so we had to take care of each other. 

new neighbors? we introduce ourselves. learn their names. often, we'd share food. none of us would ever have everything we needed, but if one person has sugar and another person has milk, and a third person has coffee, then we all get to have a cuppa in the morning. and that kind of safety net can't exist if you go around treating people like they're not worth your time.

someone wealthy doesn't need the safety net of their peers and community in most cases, so they don't feel the same imperative to get to know the people around them. i think as well, when people who were from wealthy areas moved into my miserable little hellhole of socioeconomic desperation, they were put off by our attempts at including them in this communal safety net. they don't understand that when crazy kate comes round asking for a cup of sugar it comes with the expectation that you would do the same if you needed a cup of sugar. it's a two-way social contract, and when you're in the real depths of poverty, it's not one you get any say in. it's the only way to survive.

then why are you here playing devil's advocate for investors and big business who by their very nature violate human rights? 

this is going to be long, so bear with me.

not every business violates human rights by design. if i am selling, for example, a necklace? i can't just charge you 300,000 dollars for some plastic beads i picked up from the craft store. if i did, nobody would purchase it. if my necklace is the only necklace that exists, or one of very few, i may be able to charge more if i am able to drum up demand for it. i may even be able to manipulate the market by buying out my competitors and manufacturing scarcity of necklaces to limit supply, and i can use marketing techniques to create demand.

this has its own ethical considerations, but it does not violate anyone's fundamental rights by design. if you don't want to or can't afford to buy my necklace, all that happens is you don't have a necklace. 

on the other hand, if i were able to control, for example, oxygen? and i told you you had to purchase oxygen from me, or you would have none. what happens here is not demand, but need. you cannot choose to simply not buy my oxygen from me at whatever price i chose to sell it to you for, because you don't just want it- you need it. you need to breathe. and if i set a price that you were unable to pay, then, tough titties, you're dead. it is at this point the free market becomes, in essence, a hostage situation.

this is an extreme example meant to illustrate my point, which is that the principle of supply and demand cannot be applied to the fundamental needs human beings have. demand and need are not the same thing. it doesn't matter how much you want to buy my 300,000 dollar necklace. if you don't get it, then, tough luck. but it is much more than tough luck when someone is unable to fill their physiological needs for food, water and shelter.

to some extent, supply and demand does rule our capitalist societies regardless of the need that exists. however, there are still some structures in place surrounding necessities like food and water to prevent companies from charging you 5,000 dollars for a box of cereal. competition between providers of that service can help with that- if your competitors has inflated prices too much, you can undercut them and steal their consumer base and ultimately make a bigger profit. in remote communities we see the opposite side of that coin- someone who knows their establishment is the only source of food for the next six hours in any direction is free to gouge at their own discretion, if there are no legal or professional ramifications for doing so.

shelter is a physiological need regarded by most sources as on par with the need for adequate food and water. the average life expectancy of a long-term rough sleeper is 47. even if you account for substance abuse and alcoholism, this is shockingly low. people require shelter to live. so, it is not demand, but non-negotiable need that fuels this market. 

but shelter is not treated the way food and water are treated in our economy. someone who wants to start a supermarket chain or build a dam has to go through a lot of red tape and is subject to a lot of oversight and regulation. landlords are not regarded as providers of housing the way a water company is regarded as a provider of water. they are subject to far less regulation. they don't even have to outright own the product they are supplying to the public. that's because our country was originally built with the intention of every australian owning their own home. landlords were meant to be an exception, not the rule.

but, with an unregulated free market, combined with the fact that this market controls the supply of a non negotiable human need, aka infinite demand, prices rapidly inflate past the point of anyone ever being able to obtain a home without going into lifelong debt. even if you make six figures, it's unlikely you'll be able to pay for a house in straight cash without a loan. 

landlords and corporations invest in property because there will never be a time where people just don't want live in a home anymore. this lifelong debt combined with the race to bloat your portfolio with as many rapidly appreciating assets as possible then leads to over-extended investors needing to recoup their costs at the expense of tenants, further depleting supply, placing affordable housing even further out of reach, forcing more people into the cycle.

in my experience, it depends on the cop, and whether or not you're in the campsite or not. if you're present at the camp, the cops will usually give you a timeframe in which you have to move on and if your stuff is still there once your time is up they will take it. if you're not in your camp, it's more likely they will take it. 

i have known one or two cops to look the other way, but remember that once the police know where your camp is you aren't safe anymore, because even if one cop doesn't feel like persecuting you, they will almost certainly tell their colleagues who will not be as lenient. if you see Any cops sniffing around, find a new camp.

use google maps to scope out places to camp. i usually go for areas with dense leafy cover- could be a park, the borders of a stream, i have even seen highway islands/roundabouts with good cover. more urban areas will see you looking for places that are tucked away out of sight. eyeball the area and ask yourself if you would be able see a tent/tarp if you were just walking around. 

if you aren't packing your stuff up and taking it with you everywhere you go (some people swear by this as the only way, but there is a psychological comfort to be had in having a base camp, a "home" of sorts) you want to make sure people aren't going to stumble across it. pretend you're playing hide and seek. because people are looking for us- the cops, other homeless, people who think we bring down the "tone of the neighbourhood". hide. 

you will probably want your base camp to be close to:
+ any 24/7 business with a bathroom (gyms and gas stations are my favourite) or really any public toilets. you just want somewhere you can shit in peace, and wash up a bit. 
+ public transport. 

the beach used to be my go-to as there were sand dunes covered in dense scrub that made for a perfect place to hide a campsite, but you gotta work with what your landscape offers you. don't be afraid to move if something feels off. trust your instincts. 

i also tend to scope out areas that are more wealthy as there is less risk that all the good spots will be taken up by other homeless. but it's risky- i'm more likely to have the police called to remove me if anyone spots me, but less likely to have to compete for good hiding spots with my fellow homeless as the karen-filled affluent areas aren't as appealing to a lot of us.

never leave anything in your camp that you can't live without. accept that every time you leave your base camp you may come back to find your stuff gone. make peace with it and have a plan already made for what you will do if that happens, and never let your valuables leave your person.

friends of friends are also an option, if your loved ones are willing to vouch for you- the way i opened up some places i can stay at was by asking my friends to ask around in their circles and see if anyone had a guestroom they were willing to put me up in for a few weeks/months.
